title: Phase 10: Dockerized deployment and CI/CD
description: Project: Phase 10: Dockerized deployment and CI/CD. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: The expense platform works on your machine, but production is a different environment. Docker gives you a reproducible artifact, and CI/CD gives you a repeatable path from commit to production. Without both, every deployment is a manual ceremony that depends on the engineer remembering the right sequence of steps.

Containers package an application with its runtime, dependencies, and configuration into a single artifact. That artifact runs the same way on a developer laptop, a CI runner, and a production server. The alternative—installing .NET, configuring environment variables, and copying files manually—creates environment drift that shows up as 'it works on my machine' bugs.

data.title: Containerization benefits for the expense platform
items: Consistent runtime: the same image runs in development, staging, and production
Dependency isolation: the API and background worker have their own runtime versions
Resource limits: CPU and memory constraints prevent a runaway job from starving the host
Fast spin-up: containers start in seconds, enabling rapid rollback and scaling
Immutable infrastructure: images are built once and never modified in place
Multi-stage builds: compile and publish in one stage, copy the output into a minimal runtime image
Layer caching: unchanged dependencies are cached between builds, speeding up CI

terms.definition: A read-only template containing an application and its dependencies, built from a Dockerfile.
A runnable instance of an image, with its own filesystem, network, and process space.
A Dockerfile that uses multiple FROM instructions to separate build-time dependencies from the runtime image, reducing final image size.
An intermediate read-only filesystem in an image. Docker caches layers between builds to speed up image creation.
An automated workflow that builds, tests, and deploys code when changes are merged.
A reproducible output of a build step, such as a Docker image, NuGet package, or compiled binary.

data.text: A well-written Dockerfile is small, fast to build, and secure. The expense platform API and background worker can share a base image but should have separate Dockerfiles because they run different entrypoints and may have different resource requirements.

data.title: Multi-stage Dockerfile for ASP.NET Core
data.content: Build the application in the SDK image, then copy the output into a minimal runtime image:
data.code:
# Build stage
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY ["ExpenseApi.csproj", "ExpenseApi/" ]
RUN dotnet restore "ExpenseApi/ExpenseApi.csproj"
COPY . .
WORKDIR "/src/ExpenseApi"
RUN dotnet build "ExpenseApi.csproj" -c Release -o /app/build

# Publish stage
FROM build AS publish
RUN dotnet publish "ExpenseApi.csproj" -c Release -o /app/publish /p:UseAppHost=false

# Runtime stage
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-alpine AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=publish /app/publish .
EXPOSE 8080
ENV ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://+:8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "ExpenseApi.dll"]

data.text: CI/CD is the automation that turns code commits into deployed features. A typical pipeline for the expense platform restores dependencies, runs tests, builds Docker images, pushes them to a registry, and deploys to Kubernetes or a container service. Every step should be reproducible and visible.

items: On every pull request: restore, build, run unit and integration tests, and lint.
On merge to main: build Docker images, run security scans, and push to the registry with a git SHA tag.
On deploy to staging: apply database migrations, run smoke tests, and notify the team in Slack.
On deploy to production: use a canary release or blue-green deployment with automated rollback on error rate spike.
On failure: stop the pipeline, notify the channel, and require a manual retry after root cause is identified.

data.caption: CI/CD pipeline from commit to production with quality gates
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Developer pushes PR] --> B[CI: restore, build, test]
    B --> C{Tests pass?}
    C -->|No| D[Notify: PR checks failed]
    C -->|Yes| E[Code review]
    E --> F[Merge to main]
    F --> G[Build Docker image]
    G --> H[Security scan: Trivy]
    H --> I[Push to registry]
    I --> J[Deploy to staging]
    J --> K[Smoke tests]
    K --> L{Tests pass?}
    L -->|No| M[Rollback staging]
    L -->|Yes| N[Promote to production]
    N --> O[Canary 5%]
    O --> P{Error rate stable?}
    P -->|No| Q[Rollback to previous]
    P -->|Yes| R[Full rollout]

data.title: Treat CI time as user experience
data.text: A pipeline that takes twenty minutes means engineers wait twenty minutes for feedback. Slow CI encourages large batches and bypasses the review cycle. Keep unit tests under two minutes, run integration tests in parallel, and cache dependencies aggressively.

data.text: Never hardcode secrets in Dockerfiles or CI configuration. Use a secrets manager such as Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault. Inject secrets at runtime through environment variables or mounted files, and rotate them on a schedule.

items: Store database connection strings, API keys, and JWT signing keys in a secrets manager.
Reference secrets by name in CI/CD; the pipeline fetches them at runtime.
Use separate secret stores for development, staging, and production.
Rotate secrets automatically every 90 days or immediately after a suspected leak.
Audit secret access logs to detect unauthorized usage.

items.question: How do I reduce Docker image size?
items.answer: Use multi-stage builds to separate build and runtime dependencies. Choose minimal base images such as Alpine or Distroless. Combine RUN commands to reduce layers, and use .dockerignore to exclude source code and build artifacts.

items.question: Should I build Docker images in CI or on the developer machine?
items.answer: Always build in CI. Local builds create environment drift and make it impossible to reproduce deployments. The only local Docker use should be for integration testing during development.

items.question: How do I handle database migrations in CI/CD?
items.answer: Run migrations as a separate deploy step, not inside the application startup. Use a migration tool such as Flyway or DbUp, and make the migration step idempotent. Roll back migrations before rolling back application code.

items.question: What is the difference between blue-green and canary deployments?
items.answer: Blue-green runs two identical environments and switches traffic. Canary rolls out to a small percentage of traffic first. Blue-green is faster to cut over but requires double the infrastructure. Canary is safer for large user bases because it limits blast radius.

data.title: Build a CI/CD pipeline for the expense platform
data.description: Create a GitHub Actions workflow that builds Docker images for the API and background worker, runs tests, scans for vulnerabilities, and deploys to a staging environment.
steps: Create a Dockerfile for the API using multi-stage builds
Create a Dockerfile for the background worker using multi-stage builds
Write a GitHub Actions workflow with jobs for test, build, and deploy
Add a Trivy security scan step that fails on critical vulnerabilities
Configure deployment to a staging environment with a manual approval gate
Test the pipeline by opening a PR, merging, and verifying the deployment
data.expectedOutcome: You should have a fully automated pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys the expense platform with security scanning and manual approval gates.

data.title: Summary
points: Use multi-stage Dockerfiles to keep images small and secure
Automate the entire path from commit to production with CI/CD
Gate every production deployment on passing tests and security scans
Use canary or blue-green deployments to reduce risk
Never store secrets in Dockerfiles or CI configuration
data.takeaway: Deployment should be boring. The more automated and repeatable it is, the fewer opportunities for human error.
